Reproducibility ensures re-running the same analysis yields identical results. Because a random process is involved in generating the bootstrap weights with `fwb::fwb()`, steps must be taken to ensure reproducibility is possible. As of version 0.7.0, all that is required is to call `set.seed()` before `fwb()`, replacing `{N}` with your favorite integer:

```r
set.seed({N})

f.out <- fwb(.)
```

The same procedure works for `vcovFWB()`. You do not need to select a particular random number generator, and you do not need to do anything differently when parallelizing. The rest of this guide explains what is and is not guaranteed, how to reproduce results computed by earlier versions, and what to know about the parallel backends.

### What the results depend on {#depends}

The bootstrap weights are a function of the state of the random number generator when `fwb()` is called, and nothing about *how* the work is carried out enters into them. None of the following changes your results:

- `cl`, which controls whether and how parallelization takes place, whether it is unspecified, an integer, a `cluster` object, or `"future"`

- the number of workers, or the *future* plan in use

- `verbose`, i.e., whether a progress bar is displayed

- the random number generator in effect (`RNGkind()`)

- whether the function supplied to `statistic` draws random numbers of its own

An analysis is therefore reproducible on a machine with a different number of cores, or by a collaborator who prefers a different parallel backend, and switching from `cl = 2` to `cl = "future"` to inspect a slow bootstrap costs nothing. What does determine the results is the seed together with the arguments that define the bootstrap itself: `R`, `wtype`, `strata`, `cluster`, and `simple` (see [The `simple` argument](#simple)). The single exception is described in [Using *futurize*](#futurize).

### Why this works {#why}

Before any bootstrap replication runs, `fwb()` reserves a separate random number stream for each of the `R` replications, and each replication draws its weights from the stream reserved for it. These are L'Ecuyer-CMRG streams, generated with `parallel::nextRNGStream()`. The streams are derived from the calling session's generator state, which is what `set.seed()` sets, and they are recorded in the returned object.

Two useful things follow. The weights for a given replication depend on the seed and on the replication number, and not on which worker happened to run it or in what order, so a parallel backend cannot change them. And because the seeds that generated the weights are recorded, the weights that were used can be recovered exactly rather than inferred, which is what allows `fwb.array()` to return them without the backend that produced them (see [BCa confidence intervals](#bca)).

### Reproducing results from earlier versions {#earlier}

Results from *fwb* 0.6.0 and earlier cannot be reproduced with version 0.7.0 or later when `simple = TRUE`, which is the default for every `wtype` except `"multinom"`. To reproduce a specific earlier analysis, install the version it was run under[^install]. Results with `simple = FALSE` are unchanged.

[^install]: To install a prior version of *fwb*, you can use, e.g., `pak::pak("fwb@0.6.0")`.

Previously, weights were drawn inside each bootstrap replication, from whatever random number stream the worker running it happened to have. This made the results depend on how the work was distributed, and reproducing them required arranging the workers' streams by hand. The guidance was correspondingly involved, as it depended on `cl`, on `simple`, on whether `statistic` was random, and on `verbose`, and with a `cluster` object it required `parallel::clusterSetRNGStream()` instead of `set.seed()`.

Two pieces of that guidance are worth calling out, because following them today would be counterproductive. `parallel::clusterSetRNGStream()` no longer has any effect on `fwb()`; the workers' own streams are never used to draw weights, so code that relies on it in place of `set.seed()` is not reproducible. And `set.seed(., "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")` is no longer needed, as `set.seed()` with any generator is enough. Note that different generators select different streams, so the same integer gives different (individually reproducible) results with and without the `kind` argument.

### The `simple` argument {#simple}

`simple` controls when the weights are drawn. With `simple = FALSE`, the entire `R` $\times$ $n$ weight matrix is drawn in one step before `statistic` is applied to anything. With `simple = TRUE`, each replication draws its own weights as it runs, which avoids holding the whole matrix in memory.

Both settings are fully reproducible, and both draw from the same weight distribution, so either supports valid inference. They consume their random number streams differently, though, so `simple = TRUE` and `simple = FALSE` do not yield the same replicates as each other even with the same seed. Previously they did coincide for the continuous weight types, which is worth knowing if you have code that switched between them freely. Default is `TRUE` except when `wtype = "multinom"`, where `FALSE` is used so that results match `boot::boot(., stype = "f")` exactly.

### BCa confidence intervals {#bca}

Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) intervals require the empirical influence of each unit on the bootstrap estimates, which means recovering the weights that were used. Because those weights are recorded (i.e., through the seeds that generated them), `fwb.ci(., type = "bca")` and `summary(., ci.type = "bca")` work without any preparation on your part, whatever `cl` was set to and whether or not `statistic` is random. Previously, BCa intervals were refused outright when `simple = TRUE` and `statistic` had a random component.

BCa intervals still require more bootstrap replications than there are units in the data, and still cannot be used with `cluster` (i.e., with the clustered bootstrap).

### Choosing a parallel backend {#backend}

Because the choice does not affect your results, it can be made on practical grounds. `cl` accepts an integer (which uses forking and is not available on Windows), a `cluster` object from `parallel::makeCluster()`, or the string `"future"` to use whatever backend `future::plan()` has set up. The *futurize* package offers a further route, described below.

One thing does differ between backends, and it does not concern reproducibility. A `cluster` object starts fresh R processes with no packages attached, so a `statistic` that calls functions from another package needs that package attached there, e.g., with `parallel::clusterEvalQ(cl, library(mypkg))`. *fwb* itself is attached for you, so the `w_*()` functions (e.g., `w_mean()`, `w_std()`) can be used with no extra effort. Forking and *future* backends handle this on their own. Progress reporting also differs; see [Progress bars](#progress).

### Using *futurize* {#futurize}

The *futurize* package can parallelize an `fwb()` call by piping it. See below for a code example:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(futurize)
plan(multisession)

set.seed({N})

f.out <- fwb(.) |> futurize()
```

This is reproducible in the ordinary way, and a plain `set.seed()` is all it needs. There is one wrinkle, and it is the single exception to the rule that only the seed matters: adding or removing `|> futurize()` changes the replicates. *futurize* switches the generator to L'Ecuyer-CMRG for the duration of the call, and doing so re-initializes the generator state even when L'Ecuyer-CMRG is already in use. The streams *fwb* then reserves are a deterministic function of your seed, but they are not the ones a call without the pipe would have used, so reproducing a result means reproducing whether `futurize()` was used.

See `vignette("futurize-81-fwb", package = "futurize")` for more details on using *futurize* with *fwb*.

### Progress bars {#progress}

`fwb()` displays a progress bar when `verbose = TRUE`, using the *pbapply* package. This works with every backend and, unlike in earlier versions, has no effect on the results. Default is `TRUE` when running sequentially and `FALSE` when parallelizing.

Alternatively, the *progressify* package routes progress through *progressr*, which lets you choose the reporter. See below for a code example:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(progressify)
handlers(global = TRUE)

set.seed({N})

f.out <- fwb(.) |> progressify()
```

When combining parallelization with *progressify*, a *future* backend must be used (i.e., `cl = "future"`, or the `futurize()` pipe described above), because *progressr* has no way to receive updates from a forked worker. With `cl` set to an integer or a `cluster` object, the bootstrap runs correctly but no progress is reported; use `verbose = TRUE` in that case to display a progress bar.

See `vignette("progressify-81-fwb", package = "progressify")` for more details on using *progressify* with *fwb*.

### A note on `statistic` {#statistic}

`statistic` may draw random numbers, which no longer costs anything in reproducibility, because each replication's weights are drawn from a stream reserved in advance and cannot be shifted by what `statistic` did in an earlier replication. Its own draws are reproducible for the same reason.

Two things are still worth avoiding. Do not call `set.seed()` inside `statistic`, which would give every replication the same draws. And note that a `statistic` that parallelizes internally, on top of *fwb*'s own parallelization, may not be reproducible; that is a property of the nested code and not of `fwb()`.
